abstract_text:
ABSTRACT
Cerebellar granule cells (GCs) are the most numerous neurons in the brain, and are packed densely in a single
cerebellar layer containing their relatively small somata and just a handful of dendritic processes. Classic
models propose that GCs transform diverse sensory and motor inputs into sparse activity patterns to support
pattern separation, a computation thought to underlie the cerebellum’s precision and adaptability in learning.
This transformation is often attributed to network architecture and synaptic mechanisms, but whether intrinsic
GC properties also affect pattern separation remains largely unexplored. Although GCs are traditionally viewed
as passive integrators of synaptic input, preliminary data from our lab shows that they express the sodium
channel NaV1.2 in their soma and dendrites, suggesting they may also utilize active properties to dynamically
shape how synaptic signals are processed. This raises the possibility that intrinsic conductances inﬂuence
how GCs integrate and potentially amplify excitatory input, which would inﬂuence ﬁring dynamics, and
ultimately contribute to the ﬁdelity and consistency of population-level codes. Aim 1 uses ex vivo patch-clamp
recordings and modeling in mice heterozygous for or lacking SCN2A expression entirely to determine how 50%
and 100% loss of NaV1.2 in GCs inﬂuences ﬁring properties and integration of mossy-ﬁber inputs. Aim 2 uses
in vivo two-photon calcium imaging during sensory stimulation and movement to test whether NaV1.2 loss
disrupts the precision, separability, and decoding accuracy of GC ensemble activity. Together, these
experiments will determine whether even morphologically simple neurons employ intrinsic excitability
mechanisms to inﬂuence circuit computations, advancing understanding of how cellular design supports the
cerebellum’s ability to generate precise, high-dimensional representations of sensorimotor input.
project_title: Mechanisms and Function of Dendritic Integration in Cerebellar Granule Cells
phr_text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE
Cerebellar granule cells, the brain’s most abundant neuronal cell type, offer a model for understanding how
cellular design supports circuit-level computation. This project investigates the potential role of NaV1.2 in
granule cell integration and population-level pattern separation essential for cerebellar processing. Clarifying
this relationship will test whether even morphologically simple neurons like granule cells leverage intrinsic
excitability features endowed by expressed ion channels to shape information processing.
